source_document.body:
A decision handed down by the U.S. Supreme Court Monday is setting up the possibility of a major decision on the question of shipper and recipient liability in a post-Montgomery world.
The high court granted certiorari in the case of Casarez vs. Irigoyen Farms et. al. in an action known as a Grant, Vacate, Remand Order (GVR). Unlike a more traditional certiorari finding, a granting of GVR allows the high court to send the case back to a lower court without actually ruling on its merits, but keeping open a chance the nine justices will take up the issue later.
With its GVR order, the case of Casarez vs. Irigoyen Farms will be returned to a California appellate court that will take up anew the question of whether a shipper or even their customer can be hit with liability coming out of a crash. The legal process in Casarez so far has firmly answered “no” to that question.
But that was before Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II stripped away certain protections for brokers, with the possibility that the new landscape for litigation could eventually create liability for shippers–and their customers–as well.
Had that SCOTUS certiorari grant and accompanying remand order not been issued, the case would have effectively shut down in the Golden State, with a body of decisions favorable to the shipper and recipient formulated before Montgomery turned the freight world upside down.
Biggest retailer is in the case
One of those defendants in the et. al list: Walmart (NYSE: WMT). Irigoyen was sending produce from its operations in Selma, California to a Walmart distribution center in Nevada.
Irigoyen and Walmart, in earlier decisions, were ruled to not have liability in the September 2019 crash that killed Olivia Mendoza when a truck driven by independent contractor Andre Hill, carrying produce from Irigoyen to Walmart, went through a stop sign and slammed into Mendoza’s car near Fresno. She died at the scene.
Plaintiff Casarez was Mendoza’s mother.
Hill was ultimately sentenced to two years in prison after being found guilty on a charge of vehicular manslaughter.
According to briefs filed in the case, Irigoyen had contracted with Royal Violet Logistics to arrange for the delivery of the produce. Royal Violet then contracted with SIO Logistics, who then hired Gold Coast Logistics as carrier of the load. Gold Coast hired Hill to move the freight to Walmart. .
It was not immediately clear what the outcome was of any litigation directed at the 3Pls or the carrier.
But their presence is largely irrelevant to the more significant aspect of the case. Casarez vs. Irigoyen could be groundbreaking in the ongoing post-Montgomery reckoning that will need to shake out whether the expanded legal landscape against brokers created by Montgomery might expand to include shippers–in this case Irigoyen–or even freight customers, in this case Walmart.
Winning in the lower courts
Irigoyen and Walmart, in earlier decisions in the California court system, were ruled to not have liability in the crash.
First stop for the Casarez case was Fresno County Superior Court, which in September 2023 granted summary judgment to Irigoyen and Walmart and dismissed them from the lawsuit. Their pleading was that the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act and its prohibition of a state action that could impact a “price, route or service” preempted action against the two companies.
The two defendants also argued the F4A “safety exception” that would allow torts or other action in the event of an incident like a crash could not suck them in, because Walmart and Irigoyen were not “motor vehicles.” The safety exception’s wording is that it is “with respect to motor vehicles.”
The decision in Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II ended any debate over whether the actions of brokers could be viewed under F4A as being “with respect to motor vehicles.” They can be, and in the years to come, they almost certainly will be.
Next came the Fifth Appellate District of the California Court of Appeal which in September 2025 affirmed the Fresno County court decision. Soon after, in January 2026, the California Supreme Court denied review.
A whole new world
But then Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II landed in May , undercutting much of the rationale for the findings of the two California courts. That led Casarez to petition the U.S. Supreme Court for certiorari, which was granted Monday.
A raging debate in the industry now is whether “with respect to motor vehicles” can also be used to bring a shipper or freight recipient into a lawsuit over a crash or other incident.
Casarez vs. Irigoyen Farms could be the platform for settling that question, even as shippers so far have prevailed since the ruling in Montgomery. For example, just days after the Montgomery decision, a Texas court rejected liability for Home Depot (NYSE: HD) in a fatal wreck where its products were being hauled by Werner Enterprises (NASDAQ: WERN) .
Walmart released a brief statement on the decision. “(Monday’s) order grants the relief Walmart asked for in its response to Ms. Casarez’s petition,” the company said. “We will continue to defend the company in the California Court of Appeal.”
In its brief to the Supreme Court, Walmart tried to separate itself out from the process that led Hill to be hired. “As the intended recipient of the shipment, Walmart played no role in arranging for transportation,” the company said. “Walmart did not select the broker, the motor carrier, or the driver. It did not provide or maintain the vehicle. Nor did it participate in any other way.”
Attorney Gregory Reed, a partner with the law firm of Hanson Bridgett and leader of its Transportation and Logistics practice group, wrote about the case last year after the appellate court ruling but before the California Supreme Court declined review and before Montgomery.
Case is one to watch
In an email to FreightWaves, Reed said the Walmart/Irigoyen case is “the most important shipper-receive liability case to watch right now.”
But he added that “it is unclear whether the door is open for a monumental ruling,” as occurred with Montgomery.
Reed noted that although the Supreme Court’s action keeps the case alive, for now it had “passed on taking up the question that both Irigoyen Farm and (Casarez) requested: whether F4A preemption can be invoked by parties, such as shippers and receivers further up the supply chain, other than brokers and motor carriers as expressly enumerated in the statute.”
As far as whether the certiorari grant might pave the way for later Supreme Court review, Reed said there is no circuit court split at this point on the question of shipper/receiver liability that might spur such a review.
And that lack of a circuit court consensus is often necessary for any issue to be reviewed by the nine justices. For example, after earlier certiorari rejections by the Supreme Court on the issue of broker liability, the court finally granted review in Montgomery when those split decisions began to pile up.
Second, Reed noted a distinction between Walmart and Irigoyen: the latter had driver Hill onsite where multiple people said he was visibly fatigued. That could be an issue for the produce provider, but it isn’t for Walmart.

source_document.body:
Finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky. Parents generally want something safe, manageable, and from a reputable company. Teenagers, meanwhile, generally want something that doesn’t look like it was picked out by their parents.
The newly launched Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.
The new youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm). But perhaps more importantly for parents, Juiced also built in a PIN-protected speed limiter known as Speed Lock that lets adults decide just how fast the bike can go.
The Scrambler Mini ships set to a 10 mph (16 km/h) Beginner Mode, but its maximum speed can be adjusted anywhere from 1-20 mph (32 km/h) and then locked behind a four-digit PIN. Juiced notes that riders aged 8-12 should not exceed 10 mph, while riders 13 and older can use the bike at speeds up to 20 mph, subject of course to local laws and regulations. In almost every state and jurisdiction though, the bike will fit Class 2 designation for street-legal riding and bike lane operation.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That setup seems like a pretty smart way to approach youth e-bikes. Instead of buying a slow bike that a teenager may quickly outgrow – or handing them a much faster machine before a parent thinks they’re ready – the same bike can essentially grow with the rider (with speed titrated by a parent or guardian).
And from the kid’s perspective, it certainly doesn’t look like a safety-first children’s bike.
The Scrambler Mini gets the same sort of moto-inspired styling that has defined Juiced’s Scrambler lineup , including a long bench seat, dual-crown-style fork, chunky 16 x 4-inch tires, and several appropriately loud color options including Blackberry, Fruit Punch, Blueberry, and Pink Lemonade.
There’s some decent hardware underneath that styling, too. The rear hub motor is rated at 500W nominal and 1,092W peak with 80 Nm of torque. A removable 48V 10Ah battery using LG cells provides 480Wh of capacity, with Juiced claiming up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Four levels of cadence-based pedal assist are included, as is a right-side thumb throttle.
The bike also features Talon hydraulic disc brakes with large 180mm rotors front and rear, 50mm of front suspension travel, an integrated backlit LCD, a headlight, and a rear taillight with brake-light functionality. The single-speed bike weighs 59 lb (26.8 kg), has a 27.15-inch seat height, and is rated for up to 275 lb (125 kg) of payload.
Those parts are far above what we normally see on e-bikes targeted towards teens, with most teen-focused e-bikes sporting cheaper components like mechanical brakes and rigid forks .
The Scrambler Mini is listed at $1,099 , though Juiced is currently offering a Black Friday sale that drops the price by another $150 to just $949 . The company says preorders are expected to begin shipping the week of December 7.
That price also comes with something increasingly important in the crowded youth e-bike market: an actual company standing behind the bike. Juiced was founded in 2009, quickly becoming a leader in the market for powerful and stylish e-bikes. But after the brand’s financial troubles a few years ago, Lectric eBikes stepped in to take Juiced under its wing in 2025 . The relaunched Juiced now offers a three-year manufacturer warranty and US-based support, plus the peace of mind that comes with backing from North America’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes.
That last part may be just as appealing to parents as the speed limiter, though the 3-year warranty is definitely a deal sweetener, too.
Electrek’s Take
There’s always going to be some controversy around the idea of e-bikes marketed towards teens, but I’m for it when done responsibly. Let’s face it: e-bikes are incredibly popular and teens are already going to be riding them, even if it means borrowing a friend’s e-bike because they don’t have their own. So if they’re going to be riding, the least we can do is put them on a safer, higher-quality bike so they learn the right skills in the right environment. And hey, it sure beats teens sitting alone in their rooms texting each other all afternoon.
When it comes to choosing an e-bike, there are already plenty of cheap mini e-bikes and electric dirt bike-style machines floating around online, and many are undoubtedly going to look tempting to teenagers. The Scrambler Mini seems to take a different approach, giving young riders the styling, fat tires, throttle, and mini-moto attitude they actually want, while giving parents control over how much of that performance they can access.
It’s still an e-bike capable of 20 mph, and that means parents need to make decisions about where, when, and how their kids ride it. And there’s even an argument to be made for removing the throttle and turning it into a Class 1 e-bike in the beginning, requiring a teen to pedal it to engage the motor. But I’d much rather see that conversation happening around a bike with hydraulic brakes, lights, a programmable speed limit, and a real company standing behind it than around some anonymous electric mini-bike bought from the depths of the internet.
And if the teenager thinks it looks cool enough to actually ride, that’s probably the point.

The Woodland version is bigger and more powerful than the standard Toyota bZ , and it may be a better deal right now.
Toyota bZ Woodland offers and lease deals
Toyota now sells three electric SUVs in the US ( see which one is the best fit for you ): the bZ (previously called the bZ4Z), C-HR, and bZ Woodland.
The C-HR is a smaller, sportier crossover SUV, while the bZ Woodland adds a larger, more rugged option.
Toyota is currently offering a deal on the 2026 bZ Woodland for Black Friday that might be worth a look.

The deal includes 0% APR financing for 72 months, plus an extra $1,000 Holiday Bonus Cash. Toyota said that if you finance a new 2026 bZ Woodland for 72 payments, it will cost $13.89 for every $1,000 financed.
In comparison, the standard 2026 bZ is available with 1.99% interest for 72 months at $14.75 for every $1,000 financed.
For leasing, the standard 2026 Toyota bZ is cheaper, starting at $369 per month. The deal is for a 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing for an effective cost of $490 per month.
Toyota bZ Woodland Premium (Source: Toyota)
However, that’s for the single-motor FWD version. Upgrading to AWD will cost around $606 a month for the same 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing.
Toyota is promoting 2026 bZ Woodland leases as low as $449 a month. That’s also for a 36-month lease with $4,448 due at signing.
Toyota bZ (Source: Toyota)
How they stack up
The Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower, which is 37 hp more than the standard bZ SUV with AWD.
Toyota’s standard bZ is offered with FWD and AWD powertrains. FWD models deliver either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models produce a combined 338 hp.
2027 Toyota bZ Woodland Premium interior (Source: Toyota)
The Woodland model is also 6″ longer than the standard bZ, opening up an additional 30 cubic feet of cargo space on the inside.
Toyota’s bigger SUV also adds a rugged look and off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and up to 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.
Other rugged upgrades are standard, including All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.
Inside, both come with a 7″ digital cluster and a large 14″ touchscreen running the latest Toyota Audio Multimedia system with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
Although it uses the same 74.7-kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland version offers slightly less driving range because of the added power and off-road equipment. The 2027 bZ Woodland has an estimated range of up to 281 miles with all-season tires, or 260 miles with the optional all-terrain tires.
Toyota bZ interior (Source: Toyota)
In comparison, the bZ is available with two battery packs: 57.7 kWh and 74.7 kWh. The base XLE FWD uses the 57.7 kWh battery, while the XLE AWD and FWD Plus, Limited AWD, and FWD models use the 74.7 kWh battery.
The standard 57.7 kWh battery provides an EPA range of up to 236 miles, while the 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 314 miles for FWD and 288 miles for AWD.
Both the bZ and bZ Woodland have a native NACS port, so drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. It takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.
The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

An AH-64E Apache taxis down the flight line at Hunter Army Airfield, Georgia, March 19, 2021. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Andrew McNeil, 3rd Combat Aviation Brigade, 3rd Infantry Division).
WASHINGTON — As the Army fa ces declining avi ation readiness numbers and an increase in accidents over the past year, the service’s number two civilian had a bleak message: “We have to change something.” Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal told an audience today that the service’s m anned aviation fleet’s fully mission capable (FMC) rates are sitting at “a norm” of below 60 percent — well below the service’s goal of 75 percent . Army aviators are also facing an accident rate “that’s gone up exponentially,” which Obadal linked to insufficient flight time for pilots and crews to maintain proficiency.
“We actually had more accidents this year, and we flew 150,000 hours less than we did three years ago. So more accidents, less hours, less readiness,” Obadal, a retired Army aviator, said during an AUSA Hot Topic event today. “Pilots don’t fly as much, crews don’t fly as much. Eighty two percent of our Class A accidents are human factors. I t has to change. We cannot put any more lives [into] that because we ignore the problem.”
Army aviation safety data paints a more complicated picture. Although the service’s Class A mishap rate improved in FY25, its overall Class A-C flight mishap rate was higher than in any of the previous 10 years, according to an Army newsletter [ PDF ] published in January. Class C mishaps have increased in each of the past three years, even as flying hours have declined, the newsletter noted. Obadal did not specify the types or severity of the accidents over the last year, nor did he provide specific figures.
The readiness picture has been less encouraging. Data on Army Aviation’s FY25 FMC rates is not yet available, but a Government Accountability Office report from March found that the service did not meet its FMC goals for FY24, though the report did not provide an exact rate. The Army had previously published its FY24 figures in an online newsletter, but that page is no longer available.
“What we are doing is looking at the trends, and year over year, our trends of fully mission capable are going down. We have to change something,” he said.
To improve readiness, Obadal said the Army is turning to its Weapons 360 platform, which provides real-time readiness data on the service’s major weapons systems and helps identify bottlenecks down to the part and supplier level. “The way that we sustain our major end items has been very sporadic, and it’s got about six different organizations that touch it,” he said. “So I’m pulling all of them together into an Army sustainment model.” Regarding his plan to prevent future aviation accidents, Obadal said the service is “completely changing” its aviation training base . One such effort is Flight School Next , a program to acquire a new helicopter and develop new training curriculum focused on the basic stick-and-rudder skills for helicopter pilots.
The Army is also going to transfer both commissioned and warrant officers back into aviation formations “where they belong” and “out of staff jobs” to help address the increase in accidents, Obadal said. “Our aviation is fundamental, and we have to fix it,” he said.

source_document.body:
The Stibnite gold-antimony project in central Idaho. ( Image: Amanda Stutt, MINING.COM. )
Posted By: Mining.com Staff November 17, 2026
Perpetua Resources (Nasdaq, TSX: PPTA) signed a non-binding agreement with an unnamed aerospace and defence company based in the United States to explore funding for a potential tungsten project at Stibnite in central Idaho.
The memorandum of understanding contemplates up to ($55.5 million C$79 million) in non-equity funding at the prospective partner’s discretion and a possible right for it to buy up to half of Perpetua’s future tungsten output if production goes ahead. The proposed funding falls under the company’s Industrial Tungsten Acceleration Program (I-TAP).
Early discussions with U.S. manufacturers could help Perpetua assess the material, how to process it and how to develop the deposit, president and CEO Jon Cherry said in a company statement .
Perpetua is assessing whether mineralization in the historic Stibnite Mining District and on nearby claims could support commercial tungsten production. In October, the company announced up to US$40 million in U.S. Army funding to assess whether the district could produce tungsten concentrate.
The United States has had no commercial tungsten mining since 2015, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
“Stibnite offers an opportunity to evaluate a potential American source of tungsten,” Cherry said.
Shares in Perpetua Resources rose 0.9% to $17.16 Tuesday in Nasdaq trading, valuing the company at about $2.1 billion.
Future planning
Any tungsten development would proceed separately from the approved gold-antimony mine plan and require its own environmental review and permits. Perpetua said it has yet to establish whether the tungsten could be mined commercially.
If an agreement is reached and the tungsten program is funded, Perpetua expects initial work to include exploration drilling, resource definition, metallurgical and processing testing, and design and permitting for a sloping underground access tunnel.
A potential second phase could include underground exploration and development, a preliminary economic evaluation, pilot-scale processing, and assessment of recovery circuits.
Financial services firm J.P. Morgan acted as financial adviser to Perpetua Resources in connection with the potential investment.
The U.S. Forest Service approved the mine plan for the Stibnite Gold Project in 2025. Perpetua expects a final investment decision in the first quarter of 2027. Perpetua projects average gold output of 463,000 oz. a year in the first four years and 296,000 oz. a year over the mine’s life. Probable reserves contain 4.8 million oz. of gold and 148.7 million lb. of antimony.
Under the non-binding memorandum, funding and supply rights remain optional. Any binding deal would require definitive written agreements, satisfactory due diligence and applicable approvals. Print

source_document.body:
Scout Motors Production Center in Blythewood, South Carolina (Image: Scout Motors)
Volkswagen’s revived Scout brand finally has vehicles coming off the line in South Carolina, but they’re validation units, not customer cars. Scout confirms the first deliveries of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup won’t happen until 2028.
That’s two years later than the 2026 production start the company was talking about before it even broke ground on its $2 billion factory.
The Blythewood plant is real now
According to Scout’s announcement dated November 12, construction at the Production Center north of Columbia is in its final phase and most of the manufacturing equipment is installed. The Body Shop, Paint Shop, and Assembly Shop are all being used for the first validation builds.
The Body Shop is the most automated part of the plant. Scout says more than 750 robots join roughly 160 parts into each body, laying down about 5,000 weld points per vehicle, with AI-supported weld monitoring and a metrology system checking the results. At full capacity, the shop is designed to handle about 40 vehicles per hour.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Bodies then go through an electrified paint shop before landing in final assembly, where they’re married to the chassis and get their wiring, glass, seats, and wheels.
CEO Scott Keogh is clearly happy to have something physical to point to, saying that “what we are building in Blythewood is no longer a promise on paper.”
Scout also shared photos of a Terra pickup and a Traveler parked inside the plant. Its own fine print notes that they show “concept and validation vehicles” with optional features, so don’t read too much into what’s on display:
View this post on Instagram
Fair enough. But Scout is also careful about what this stage is. Teams are confirming the equipment is installed and works, and checking engineering, buildability, and parts maturity. Process validation and scaling up to production speed come later. Validation builds will continue “into 2027,” followed by pre-production builds, and then customer deliveries in 2028.
The company says the plant will create more than 4,000 jobs, and it’s spending another $300 million on an onsite supplier park expected to support about 1,000 supplier jobs.
The timeline keeps sliding
When Keogh laid out the plan in late 2023, Scout said it would start production in 2026 with deliveries shortly after. That was still the target when Scout broke ground in Blythewood in February 2024.
By the Traveler and Terra unveiling in October 2024 , production had moved to 2027. Keogh then said in March that he expects the first customer to get a vehicle “sometime in 2028,” and that’s now the official line in Scout’s own press materials.
It might not even be the end of it. Industry forecaster AutoForecast Solutions has the Traveler starting production in September 2028 and the Terra in March 2030. Scout hasn’t confirmed those dates, but it hasn’t given more precise ones either.
The product itself has also changed under the hood. Scout launched as a pure EV brand, then added the “Harvester” range-extender option at the reveal. According to Keogh, Scout has more than 160,000 reservations, and 87% of them are for the gas-generator version. Those are $100 refundable reservations, not orders.
Der Spiegel reported earlier this year that integrating the range extender, which wasn’t part of the original plan, was among the technical problems pushing the timeline back.
For comparison, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 and delivered the first ones four years later, a delay that was widely mocked. Scout is now on a similar four-year path from reveal to customer, and that’s for the SUV it’s launching first.
Electrek’s Take
A working body shop with 750 robots isn’t vaporware. Scout has a real factory, a real workforce, and two vehicles that people clearly want. 160,000 reservations is a big number for a brand that hasn’t sold a single vehicle in 46 years.
But validation builds are an early step, not a finish line. Scout still has to go through pre-production, prove its processes, and ramp to rate, and every one of those stages is where new automakers usually lose time. Rivian and Lucid both learned that the hard way.
And the market Scout was designed for in 2022 no longer exists. The EV tax credit is gone, and most of Scout’s own reservation holders picked the gas generator. In the US, the range-extender market is still early, unlike in China, where they are already popular.
But by 2028, Ford, Ram, and Jeep all plan to have range-extended trucks and SUVs on sale. Scout’s main advantage was being early with a cool, rugged, American-built electric truck. That advantage shrinks every quarter.
We’re still rooting for these vehicles. The Traveler and Terra are among the best-looking designs in the segment. But a $100 reservation is easy to walk away from, and the question is how many of those 160,000 people are still waiting in 2028.

source_document.body:
Waymo has pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after the California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the company to pause highway operation in the state, following a viral video showing a Waymo trying to pass a police blockade.
Waymo is Google’s robotaxi subsidiary, which has been operating autonomously on public roads in some form since 2017. It has now expanded to 15 areas, recently adding another 250 square miles just last month .
The vehicles can be hailed through Waymo’s app, and operate with no driver in the driver’s seat, 24/7 in the covered areas. Since it can operate at any time but only within geofenced areas, this counts as “level 4” autonomy , as compared to the level 2 autonomy available on most consumer vehicles.
Until recently, Waymo only operated on city streets. These are more complex than highways, but lower speed. Accidents are more common on city streets than on highways, but can be more spectacular on highways given the higher speeds involved.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Most driver assist systems have been rolled out gradually, starting with highways, due to this lower complexity. But Waymo started with city streets first, bucking that trend.
The company started offering rides on highways late last year, but only in limited markets. It had been testing highway operation for several years prior, typically with a driver and with no public ridership.
Everything was going pretty well, with Waymo declaring its autonomous vehicles have stopped 841 injuries over the course of their 271 million miles of operation. And in terms of competition, Waymo is far ahead of Tesla’s Robotaxi effort .
But then, the viral internet stepped in. Last week, a video surfaced showing a Waymo trying to pass two police cars who were trying to slow down traffic on I-280 in Northern California. This is one of the main routes through Silicon Valley, and the opening of highway operations drastically reduced ride times in the area.
The video shows two police cars behind a construction vehicle, lights on and spread out across the freeway. Then it pans to show a Waymo vehicle moving quickly in the far left lane. One of the officers accelerates and swerves in front of the Waymo vehicle, at which point the Waymo swerves and slows down. (One media citation says that the video seems to have been sped up by the original poster, but we’ve embedded the short local news report on it above).
In response to this, the California DMV contacted Waymo and ordered the company to pause highway operations while it examines the incident. The order was made on November 11, but wasn’t reported until today.
The DMV cited multiple instances of Waymo vehicles incurring into construction zones, not simply the one viral clip above. It said that previous incidents had occurred and been noted, and corrective actions were implemented, but that the incidents keep happening.
DMV’s pause will remain until Waymo can demonstrate “effective corrective actions” have been taken.
While the DMV’s order only applies to California highways, Waymo also paused highway operations in other states.
Waymo noted that the incidents did not involve injury or collisions, but that it will work with the DMV and other states to hopefully resume highway operations once the problem is solved.

ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio’s expansion into the U.S. missile business.
The proposed deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the U.S. and China.
“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said Iceye on Tuesday.
The firm said it would invest €1 billion in Avio in Italy over five years in a bid to expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.
The Finnish government backed the offer, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen stating, “If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe’s defense will rise to a new level.”
Avio said on Tuesday it was considering the offer, while the CEO of Italian state controlled defense group Leonardo, which owns an 18% percent stake in Avio, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would consider it.
Avio’s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which Iceye said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.
Apart from its European space launch activity, Avio is also a market leader in solid rocket motors for missiles. In September it broke ground in Hurt, Virginia, on a new U..S facility to fulfill an ambition to bring much needed extra capacity to U.S. missile production.
Avio has already partnered with Raytheon on production of the Mk 104 dual-thrust rocket motor and has teamed with Lockheed Martin to produce motors at Hurt for Lockheed’s Extended Range GMLRS (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) programs.
An Avio spokesman told Defense News that U.S. government approval would be required in the event of a takeover by Iceye, as well as Italian government approval.
In September, Avio announced a nine month order intake of €237 million, of which half was defense related, with the remainder mainly related to its Vega C and Vega E launchers.
Iceye said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.
Iceye has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.
Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.
“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities … bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.

Winter brings some of the busiest months of the year for loggers in northern Wisconsin. Frozen ground lets loaded trucks reach deeper into the woods and haul timber miles off-road to the mill. Western Star’s latest video follows one of those trucks.
The second episode of the brand’s “On the Job” series, released Nov. 12 , rides along with Nate Tessmer, owner-operator of Tessmer Trucking in Antigo, Wisconsin. His truck is a 49X, which Western Star designed with input from timber, quarry and oilfield workers .
The series also sells the vocational lineup that parent Daimler Truck North America is counting on to grow. DTNA held 24% of the heavy vocational market in 2024, the company said in its Capital Markets Day release . It is aiming for 35% by 2030, Transport Topics reported from the event .
Western Star built the series around the people who run those trucks. “Behind every demanding vocational job is someone whose skill and experience make that work possible,” Alex Martin-Banzer, Western Star brand manager, said in the release. “We created ‘On the Job’ to give those customers a platform and help people understand what their work really takes.”
Hauling timber on frozen Wisconsin roads
Tessmer’s day runs from the highway onto remote logging roads. He positions the truck for loading, manages its weight and hauls timber to different mills depending on species and destination, according to the release.
His six-axle 49X is configured for a gross vehicle weight of up to 98,000 pounds. On the day of filming, he hauled close to 60,000 pounds of timber.
“You want to get as much as you can on that payload, because that’s how you get paid,” Tessmer said in the release. “You want to be right up to the legal limit.”
Winter changes the math on Wisconsin’s state highways. Once the ground freezes at least 18 inches deep, the Wisconsin Department of Transportation can declare frozen roads . Log trucks with at least five axles can then run at up to 98,000 pounds gross, up from the normal 80,000.
No special permit is needed, but the trucks must be licensed at 80,000 pounds. The higher weights do not apply on county or local roads unless the local agency allows them.
The declaration normally runs from December to late February or early March, acco r di n g to WisDOT . Spring thaw restrictions on weaker state roads typically follow from early March into May.
Tessmer’s truck runs an 18-speed manual transmission and is set to switch to a Detroit DT12-V automated manual, according to Western Star’s episode page . Detroit introduced its DT12 vocational transmissions alongside the 49X in 2020 . Those transmissions launched with an Off-Road Mode for terrain like logging roads.
“This thing has been awesome,” Tessmer said. “I’ve had it for over a year. I’ve got 118,000 miles on it. It’s built to be in the woods.”
The 47X gives the X-Series a shorter option
The 49X has a smaller cousin. Western Star introduced the 47X in 2021 , and it shares a chassis and electrical architecture with the 49X. It measures 10 inches shorter from bumper to back of cab, which suits jobs like drywall delivery that call for a shorter truck.
The series opened with that truck. Episode one featured Dealers Supply Co., a fourth-generation, family-owned roofing distributor in Portland, Oregon. Its 47X boom truck carries a 40-foot body and a truck-mounted crane for deliveries to tight city jobsites.
The brand’s on-highway tractor is gone. DTNA retired the Western Star 57X, Transport Topics reported in March . In a statement to the outlet, the company said “the 47X and 49X reception has exceeded expectations.”
Daimler builds around vocational trucks
John O’Leary, DTNA president and CEO, made the case for the vocational push at Daimler Truck’s 2025 Capital Markets Day. “The combination of the vocational market’s lower cyclicality and the growth of our service business will further enhance our resilience, long-term growth and overall profitability,” he said in the company’s release.
DTNA also plans to build its largest U.S. truck plant for vocational and on-highway models, with operations targeted for 2029.
The 49X is picking up driverless work, too. Kodiak AI delivered two driverless Western Star 49Xs to Atlas Energy Solutions in September. Kodiak says they are the first driverless day cabs in commercial service.
Kodiak plans to deliver 65 Western Stars toward Atlas’ initial order for 100 driverless trucks. Atlas expects its driverless fleet to reach 100 trucks by mid-2027 .
But Daimler Truck does not report Western Star or vocational sales separately. Its third-quarter report and Nov. 6 earnings call did not update the 24% share figure.
Future episodes will move into more vocational applications across North America, Western Star said.
“We want our customers to demonstrate the knowledge and experience they bring to the job, the challenges they take on every day and how their Western Star helps them keep moving,” Martin-Banzer said.
Why it matters: Vocational market share remains an attractive growth opportunity for OEMs to diversify their on-highway exposure. With more stable vocational demand, higher market share leads to higher orders and more predictable revenue compared to the Class 8 on-highway segment which is more exposed to freight market boom and bust cycles.

Sailors attached to Expeditionary Medical Force One participate in an emergency room simulation during Operation Northern Lights. Northern Lights is an annual Navy Reserve Medical training exercise hosted at Fort McCoy, Wis. by Expeditionary Medical Facility Great Lakes One, a Navy Reserve expeditionary medical unit based out of Great Lakes, Ill. The purpose of this training exercise is to provide practical experience in the Expeditionary Medical Facility environment. There is classroom instruction, simulated training and practical experience in field hospital operation and patient care services. (US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class John Sorensen/Released).
As AI and biotech converge, the central question is no longer simply whether the military can collect biological data. The question is how.
Who controls collection? Under what conditions may the data be transmitted? Who is permitted to interpret them? What authority should those interpreters carry in command decisions? I contend that the Pentagon — and, in the last resort, Congress — must govern biodata as an emerging factor in not just military medicine, but in command decisions. Its confidentiality, integrity, availability and operational use are increasingly matters of force protection and command responsibility.
Emerging technologies can collect and interpret indicators of fatigue, cognitive overload, physiological stress, environmental exposure and recovery. The underlying data may include heart rate and variability, sleep and recovery measures, body temperature, blood chemistry, biomarkers of injury or infection and indicators of physiological stress, as well as less obviously medical metrics like movement and activity patterns.
Used responsibly, these capabilities could help commanders anticipate declining endurance, manage force rotations, prioritize limited medical resources and make better-informed decisions about operational readiness. But the same information, in the wrong hands or just mishandled, can expose a unit’s vulnerabilities or distort the decisions on which its mission depends.
There is a critical distinction to make here between raw data and what is done with it, by whom. A sensor measures something; an AI system interprets what that measurement may mean; a commander decides whether that assessment matters to a particular mission. These are different functions, carrying different standards of reliability and responsibility. A heart-rate measurement is not a diagnosis. A sleep deficit is not a complete measure of judgment. A model-generated readiness score is not an order, nor should it become one by default. Human judgment remains essential and humans must be held accountable for their judgments — or for their blind deference to a machine.
So how can the military use biodata right? To start with, during training, biodata could help identify accumulated fatigue, optimize recovery schedules, evaluate exposure to environmental hazards and support earlier medical assessment. Longitudinal data collected over months and years can establish an individual’s baseline, allowing clinicians to assess deviations from that person’s individual range, rather than compare every service member against an undifferentiated population average. Such uses can improve health, training design and force preservation before a deployment begins.
Moving beyond individual health, AI could identify changes in performance across a unit, help anticipate demand for medical services, or inform decisions about when a unit needs to rest and when it can keep operating. When fused with other, more traditional military data — like personnel availability, ammunition stocks, equipment status, intelligence and mission requirements — biodata becomes part of the commander’s broader operational picture.
That increases both the utility and the risk. Medical information becomes command information when an inference about the body begins to influence where, when and how a person or formation is employed. At that point, the military must be able to distinguish legitimate operational awareness from inappropriate surveillance, and decision support from human judgment blindly bowing to a statistical estimate.
Security And Privacy
Before a commander asks what a wearable device can reveal about personnel, a more basic question must be answered: Should that device be active in this environment at all?
In 2018, the Defense Department restricted geolocation capabilities in designated operational areas , recognizing that fitness trackers and related devices could expose personnel locations, routines and force concentrations.
Even data collected during peacetime can create a security risk. Over time, measurements may reveal who trains together, how long units take to recover, how long personnel remain at a facility and when readiness appears to deteriorate. A persistent record of routine behavior can become a map of future military capability — for our own planning or, if leaked, for an adversary’s.
Precisely because biodata is operationally useful, it is also worth stealing or manipulating. An adversary able to access physiological, behavioral and performance data could identify training cycles, recovery windows, deployment patterns, or possible gaps in unit endurance. Or, instead of just stealing biodata, an adversary could alter it, making a capable formation appear unfit for operations or portraying an exhausted unit as ready, which could gaslight commanders to push tired personnel beyond their limits or prematurely withdraw high-functioning forces.
Even security measures can be revealing: If everyone in a given unit turns off their trackers at once, that itself is a signal they’re likely about to be deployed. Restrictions on devices must cover the entire life cycle of the data, not simply the moment of contact.
In short, a personal health tracker may have implications well beyond its individual user — and simply turning off location sharing, or setting a device on “airplane mode,” does not necessarily eliminate the risk.
So the question for commanders is not simply whether a device is approved for purchase or useful during training. It is who has authority to permit, forbid, or restrict the device when security conditions change. A tracker that is valuable during a rehabilitation program or garrison training may be unacceptable near a sensitive installation, during preparations for deployment, or in a conflict zone. Permissions should be specific to the mission and environment, with explicit distinctions between collecting data locally, transmitting it wirelessly, and uploading it to cloud services. In some settings, the correct command decision will be to leave the device behind.
When Medical Information Becomes Command Authority
A second set of questions concerns permissions, identifiability and interpretation: Who can do what, when? Can medical professionals, military superiors and the service members themselves all see the same information? May a commander access an individual’s clinical indicators, or only an operationally relevant summary? Who may share, retain, challenge, or delete a record?
These distinctions must be designed into the policy and the technology, not tacked on ad hoc. Medical staff may need a servicemember’s personal, identifiable information for diagnosis and treatment. A commander may only need a bounded assessment of mission-relevant limitations like fatigue or illness, without access to a full medical history. The individual should have a way to understand how their information is used —and to contest misuse.
Baseline comparisons create another challenge. Comparing a service member with their own validated baseline may be more informative than measuring them against generalized averages across large populations. But illness, local environments, new equipment and incomplete measurements can alter what counts as “normal.” Rather than rubberstamp assessments they don’t understand, commanders should know whether any given assessment reflects a direct measurement, a deviation from an individual baseline, a population-based inference, or an AI-generated prediction and whether the model has been validated for the mission at hand.
AI can illuminate aspects of the problem, but it cannot by itself settle questions of unit cohesion, tactical adaptability, or military necessity. Users must guard against “automation bias,” where humans defer uncritically to computer outputs as if to an oracle, and “metric fixation,” where the ability to measure a few factors leads to ignoring important intangibles. Biological measurements should inform, not silently substitute for, professional military judgment and clinical expertise.
An AI-generated finding can appear more precise than the underlying evidence actually is. Consider a dashboard reporting that a service member is “90 percent ready.” Ready for what task, for how long, under what environmental conditions and according to which validated criteria? A numerical score may compress complex uncertainties into an illusion of simplistic certainty.
Assessments should therefore distinguish between actual measurements, diagnoses based on that hard data and predictions based on those diagnoses, with clear caveats about the uncertainty and limits inherent in any mathematical model. They should also permit a human to challenge and correct potential errors. A clinical judgment, a service member’s report, or a commander’s direct observation may reveal conditions that the model did not capture.
Recommendations: Securing the Biodata Architecture
Overall, a coherent approach to biodata should treat the following factors, not as afterthoughts, but as central to the design of the system:
First, data collection and emissions control must be explicit command decisions. Establish mission-specific rules, designate the authority to issue exceptions and require documented risk assessments for sensitive operations or locations. Build the system to degrade gracefully instead of collapsing as soon as an enemy disrupts the network. Never assume that equipment suitable for peacetime training is suitable for operational deployment.
Second, protect biodata for both individual privacy and operational security. Apply safeguards proportionate to the mission context and the value an adversary could derive from aggregation and correlation with other data. Secure the data pathway end-to-end, starting with vetted sensors and ending with strict rules for long-term retention or storage.
Third, separate clinical access from command use. Establish clear and different levels of access for medical personnel, commanders, analysts and service members. Military leaders should receive the minimum personal information necessary for legitimate decisions, while clinical determinations remain with medical professionals. Specify who may activate monitoring systems, inspect identifiable records, approve secondary uses and audit access.
Fourth, guard against blind trust in algorithmic claims. Require outputs to distinguish individual baselines from population norms, direct observations from predictions and validated results from uncertain inferences. Build in procedures for challenging a score, documenting overrides, correcting errors and preventing unjustified decisions based on incomplete data.
Fifth, assign accountability before operational adoption. Identify who approves new technologies, sets performance thresholds, adjudicates conflicting assessments, reviews risks and investigates failures. Responsibility must remain traceable to identifiable, individual humans.
Finally, train for biodata denial, deception and manipulation. In wargames, present commanders with seemingly credible readiness estimates that conflict with what their medical team, their subordinates, or their own eyes are telling them. Scenarios should include personal trackers transmitting during an exercise, improperly anonymized records exposing a small unit, or an AI tool producing corrupted conclusions. The objective is to develop judgment about when to trust an assessment, when to question it and when to operate without it.
The United States has an opportunity to use AI and biotechnology to strengthen medical care, personnel readiness and military effectiveness. Realizing that potential requires more than deploying sensors or buying analytics. It requires institutions capable of governing when information is created, where it flows, who can interpret it and how much authority it should have over consequential decisions.
Protecting both individual warfighters and the force as a whole requires protecting both the information drawn from the human body and human authority over how it is used. Biodata security is not simply a privacy issue or a medical-technology problem. It is a requirement of force protection, operational resilience and leadership.
Dr. Elise G. Annett is a Research Fellow in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare at the Institute for National Strategic Studies, National Defense University, and a Senior Digital Domain Fellow at the Center for the Application of Grand Strategy.

Ahead of a Wednesday filing deadline for public comments, Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern used their third-quarter 2026 earnings calls to argue that their controversial proposed merger would lower supply-chain costs and help railroads win freight from trucks.
Their competitors offered different responses. CPKC (NYSE: CP ) demanded rejection by the Surface Transportation Board ; CSX (NASDAQ: CSX ) emphasized partnerships, and CN (NYSE: CNI ) highlighted an agreement intended to protect its business while opening new markets.
BNSF, which as a unit of Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK-B ) doesn’t hold an earnings call, earlier offered a public statement from its chief executive opposing the merger.
The STB is expected to render a decision in 2027.
Union Pacific: Lower costs, faster service and confidence in approval
On Union Pacific’s October 22 earnings call (NYSE: UNP ), Chief Executive Jim Vena argued that combining the two networks would reduce the friction involved in moving freight between railroads.
“Our merger … will deliver substantial measurable benefits by strengthening the supply chain,” Vena said. “It will lower transportation costs and provide faster, more seamless rail service options that enable our customers to compete and help keep goods affordable for American … consumers.”
Vena characterized the transaction as an end-to-end combination with limited overlap, rather than a consolidation of substantially parallel networks. He also pushed back against competitors seeking concessions, saying requests needed to be grounded in the merger’s actual competitive effects. Chief Financial Officer Jennifer Hamann said UP (NYSE: UNP) was building cash reserves in anticipation of closing on the deal in the second half of 2027.
Norfolk Southern: Make truck-to-rail gains permanent
Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC) CEO Mark George framed the merger as a structural answer to an industry problem. Freight can shift to rail when trucking becomes expensive, then return to highways when market conditions change.
“When shippers are given a rail product that offers better value than the highway, they move freight to rail quickly, and the Union Pacific-Norfolk Southern combination is designed to create those conditions permanently,” George said on the company’s October 22 earnings call.
George acknowledged that competing railroads were already responding with new services and closer cooperation.
“We have definitely seen a more enhanced competitive environment,” he said, adding that railroads working together was good for the industry even when it made competition tougher for Norfolk Southern. His argument was that a unified network could help preserve market-share gains that otherwise might disappear as fuel prices and trucking capacity normalize.
CPKC: Reject the merger, rather than bargain over concessions
CPKC CEO Keith Creel delivered the most forceful earnings-call opposition, arguing that the proposed railroad’s scale and market power would create risks that were unnecessary.
“We don’t want a condition. We don’t want a concession. We don’t think it’s needed,” Creel said during CPKC’s October 28 earnings call, reported by Trains. “To create something that represents that much risk, that much market power forever is completely unneeded.”
Creel rejected comparisons with CPKC’s own merger, stressing that Canadian Pacific and Kansas City Southern had been the two smallest Class I systems and remained the smallest combined network. CPKC’s preferred outcome was rejection; if regulators nevertheless approved the transaction, it would seek protections including competitive access and meaningful safeguards at interchange gateways.
CSX: Partnerships can improve service without common ownership
On CSX’s October 21 earnings call, in response to a question regarding how the railroad’s partnerships with other carriers served as a counterweight to the proposed Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern combination, Chief Commercial Officer Maryclare Kenney emphasized that cooperation across railroad boundaries was established practice, not a new response invented for the merger fight.
“It’s been common practice for CSX to work closely with our interline partners to try to find new and in some cases better solutions for our customers,” Kenney said. “We’re always looking for ways across our lines of business—but I would say in particular when you think about intermodal —trying to find solutions that improve transit and improve reliability for our customers.”
Her answer focused on the commercial alternative to consolidation by connecting separate networks through service agreements. “We’ve been happy with the results we’ve seen with the partnerships we formed over the last several years, and we’ll continue to work on those going forward,” she said.
Canadian National: Protect the network and pursue Mexico growth
Canadian National CEO Tracy Robinson described its prospective agreement with Union Pacific as both a defensive measure and a growth opportunity.
“It mitigates the risk of the merger to our network and our business, but it also creates opportunities,” Robinson said on CN’s October 30 earnings call.
In her prepared remarks, Robinson said the “soon-to-be-finalized agreement” would extend CN’s reach into Mexico and position it to compete for a larger share of approximately $45 billion in annual Canada–Mexico trade. The agreement barters access in exchange for CN dropping its opposition to the merger.
BNSF: A warning about rates and reduced competition
BNSF President and CEO Katie Farmer opposed the transaction in a July 28 public statement responding to supplemental merger information submitted to regulators.
“The additional data submitted by UP does not change the fact that this would be an anti-competitive transaction between two financially healthy companies, that will raise rates on rail customers and result in higher prices for consumers,” Farmer said.
Why it matters: The outcome of the proposed merger is likely to reshape freight routings, interchange access and competitive leverage well beyond the two merging railroads.
